content.thinking:
I'm drafting the postmortem, starting with the symptom: many more customers' purchases were held for fraud review, with no rise in errors. I'm now laying out the causal chain, beginning with the alert label that flagged the change.

I'm now working through the causal steps: the pod that started at onset ran on a different node type than its peers, and I've ruled out deploys and flag changes as the cause.

I'm checking the earlier-change candidates against the reads: no deploys or flag changes turned up, and every replica is on one revision. I'm now testing whether the A100 placement can explain the different decision, looking at how the scorer rounds its operands under TF32.

I'm now settling on the causal chain: the symptom first, then the one replica that started on an A100 while its peers ran on V100, which I'll tie to the scoring code's reduced-precision rounding on that card.

I'm now writing the root cause: the fraud scorer's logit rounds its operands to TF32 on the A100, and since that logit is a small difference of two large products, the rounding turns the hold decision into mostly error.

I'm now going over the remaining postmortem sections: the still-at-risk note, which says the scoring code could again hold many more purchases on any replica that lands on an A100 card, and the start of the contributing factors, about nothing checking whether the model tolerates TF32 rounding.

I'm weighing whether the placement factor belongs in the contributing factors: the scheduler could put a replica on a different card than its peers, and the fix that held pods to V100 addresses exactly that.

I'm settling on the two contributing factors: first, nothing constrained the scheduler to one card type, so a replica could land on an A100 while its peers ran on V100, and I'll propose recording the V100 hold in the deployment manifest so auto-sync doesn't undo it. Second, no test exercised scoring on Ampere, so the precision difference went uncaught before production.

I'm now listing the contributing factors, starting with the placement gap: nothing held the service's pods to one card type, so a replica could land on an A100 while its peers ran on V100. I'm weighing a manifest change that records the V100 hold so automatic sync doesn't undo it.

I'm weighing whether being paged would have made any difference: the alert did fire, and Argus still brought the change back quickly, so I'd list the missing page as a finding rather than a contributing factor. For detection, the alert watches the aggregate ratio and not per-replica divergence by accelerator, but I can't tell whether a narrower alert would have fired sooner, so I'll leave it out.

I'm now weighing the action items: pinning the placement in the repo manifest to answer the placement gap, running the scorer tests on every accelerator type to answer the missing Ampere coverage, and routing the high-hold alert to on-call paging, which answers no factor directly.

I'm listing the went-well items now: the investigator's record of which card each replica ran on, the Mitigation Agent holding the pods to V100 and then confirming the service was back below the incident's level, Code-Fix's draft PR, and Argus ruling out flag changes from the provider history. For what went wrong, I'm noting that nobody was paged, and leaving out the logs point since that describes what the record shows rather than a failure. Finally, I'm weighing the got-lucky item: only one of the three replicas landed on an A100, so only part of the traffic was affected, and I'm checking whether that was chance.

I'm checking whether the one replica placed on an A100 is the only exposure, and I'm weighing how to phrase that its peers stayed on V100 cards and kept making their usual decisions.

I'm checking the assumptions: the rise in held purchases is attributed to the single A100 replica without having read its per-replica metrics, and the precision mechanism itself was never run. I'm also noting that the running revision is still unnamed, and then I'm starting the symptom section of the postmortem with the held-for-review rise and no matching increase in failed requests.

I'm checking the remaining step details against the record: the deploy and flag-change checks, and that the timeline entries for the went-well items each start with the agent that did the work.

action_items.item: Put the hold of io-shop's pods to Tesla-V100-SXM2-16GB cards into the repository's deployment manifest, so that turning automatic sync back on keeps it in place.
Run the fraud scorer's tests on every accelerator type present in the cluster's node pools as part of CI, and block a new accelerator type from taking io-shop replicas until they pass there.
Route FraudHoldsHigh on io-shop to an on-call rotation so that a person is paged when it fires.

causal_chain.step: Many more customers' purchases than usual were held for fraud review instead of going straight through. The share of failed requests did not rise.

ruled_out.what: A deploy or release of io-shop: no production changes came back for the day before the onset.
A mix of code revisions across replicas: all replicas ran one revision when T10 read them.
A feature-flag change: the flag provider showed no flag changes by anyone but Argus in the hour before {T13.4}.

causal_chain.step: Why: the replica io-shop-7d9c4f8b6-x2k9p had started at the onset on an NVIDIA-A100-SXM4-40GB card, while the other replicas ran on Tesla-V100-SXM2-16GB cards. T7 recorded this at {T7.1}. The service's pods had not been held to any one kind of card.

Why that placement changed the decisions: on an A100 card, the fraud scorer in the files Code-Fix read likely does its arithmetic at reduced (TF32) precision, and its hold decision does not survive that precision.

input.cause_in_plain_words: When one copy of the shop's service started on a newer kind of graphics card, its fraud check likely did its arithmetic less precisely there, so that copy put many more purchases on hold than the copies on the older cards.

contributing_factors.factor: io-shop's pods were not held to any one kind of accelerator, so the scheduler could start a replica on an A100 card next to replicas on V100 cards.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The new replica would have started on a V100 card like its peers and made the same hold decisions, so the hold share would not have risen.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: No test of the fraud scorer on Ampere cards was seen. The test file's docstring said Ampere behaviour was deliberately left untested, so how the scorer behaves on an A100 was not checked before an A100 node could take a replica.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A test that ran the scorer on an A100 would have shown its decisions differing from the V100's before any production replica landed there.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

got_lucky: Only the replica io-shop-7d9c4f8b6-x2k9p was placed on an A100 card. Its peers stayed on V100 cards, so the purchases they scored were not affected.

went_well.item: The Investigator Agent recorded which card each replica ran on and saw that io-shop-7d9c4f8b6-x2k9p had started on an A100 card at the onset.
Argus read the flag provider's history and found no flag changes by anyone else.
The Mitigation Agent held io-shop's pods to Tesla-V100-SXM2-16GB cards, a change that can be put back.
The Mitigation Agent judged the action confirmed after it saw the service no longer at the incident's level.
The Code-Fix Agent proposed a fix as draft pull request #444 for a person to review.

went_wrong: Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to the FraudHoldsHigh alert.

input.root_cause: In src/io_shop/fraud_scoring.py, `fraud_logit` rounds every operand to TF32 through `_to_tf32` when `ALLOW_TF32` is True and the accelerator is in `TF32_ACCELERATORS`, which holds "NVIDIA-A100-SXM4-40GB". The model's logit is the small difference between two large products of opposite sign, so this rounding changes each product by more than the difference the decision depends on, and on an A100 the hold decision is mostly rounding error.
input.still_at_risk: The scoring code still in place could again hold many more purchases for review on any io-shop replica that runs on an NVIDIA A100 card.
input.symptom: Many more customers' purchases were held for fraud review
